submission.natural_language_explanation: The negative pole fires retrospectively on the token that states a reported value on a scale: the score, grade, rating, rank/ordinal, percentage or proportion, level, size, version, price, status word or evaluative verdict that a record, rating or measurement assigns (e.g. 'pending' in 'Status: pending', '3' in 'rated 3 out of 5', 'third' in 'came third in the marathon', 'A' in 'their rating is A', 'significant' in 'the results were significant'), with the peak on the value word itself, not on the label that names the scale. It stays at the ~0.2 prompt baseline when a numeral or adjective merely describes one object or scene in ordinary narrative prose ('the tower is 300 metres tall', 'the package weighs 2 kilograms', 'the meeting lasted 45 minutes', 'the wooden door was green'), so it detects a value read off a scale rather than numbers or adjectives as such.

Those with body mass index (BMI) ≥ 25 had a higher frequency of ICU admission. Males had a 4.4 (95% CI 1.58, 12.308) odds of ICU admission (p = 0.0047). Those who developed acute kidney injury (AKI) and BMI 25–29.9 were strong predictors of ICU admission (p < 0.001 and p = 0.0020, respectively). Those with at least one reported comorbidity had 1.98 increased odds (95% CI 1.313, 2.99) of an ICU admission. Conclusion Findings show that age, AKI, and male sex were the strongest predictors of COVID-19 ICU admissions in the primarily Latinx population at the U.S.-Mexico border. These predictors are also likely driven by socioeconomic inequalities which are most apparent in border hospitals. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s40615-022-01478-1.


Introduction
The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic has revealed sweeping health care inequalities across the United States (U.S.). Latinx, the largest ethnic minority population in the country, has been particularly affected by severe COVID-19 complications and high mortality rates [1,2]. Latinx patients accounted for almost 1.9 times the case rate, 2.8 times the hospitalization rate, and 2.3 times the death rate compared with their White, non-Latinx counterparts in the U.S. [1]. In June 2020, during the second surge of COVID-19, the Latinx population accounted for 45% of the total number of deaths due to COVID-19 in California [3].
